note.title: The Paper Strip
note.text: In the silk town of Lyon, weaving a pattern was slow: before every pass of the shuttle, a helper had to pull the cords of the right threads by hand. In 1725 Basile Bouchon, whose father built organs, gave the loom a long strip of paper punched with holes instead. The holes chose which threads would lift, one row of holes for each row of cloth. For the first time, a loom read its own pattern.

note.title: A Cheap Purple
note.text: For two thousand years purple was the dearest dye there was: Tyrian purple was squeezed from thousands of sea snails, and only emperors could afford to wear it. In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old student trying to make a medicine at home, found a purple dye in coal tar instead. He called it mauve, and his factory made it by the barrel, cheaply. Within a few years anyone could wear purple, and chemists set out to make every dye that way.

note.title: Cards on a Chain
note.text: A paper strip is hard to change once it's punched. In 1728 Jean-Baptiste Falcon, who worked with Bouchon, cut the pattern into cards and laced them together in a chain. A card could be mended, swapped or moved without punching the whole pattern again. Your pattern cards carry the same idea: the picture comes into the machine on a card.

note.title: The Drawloom
note.text: Long before cards, weavers in China wove pictures into silk on the drawloom. A helper sat high on the loom and pulled cords, one bundle for each row, to lift the threads the picture needed. In 2013 archaeologists in Chengdu found four small wooden models of such looms in a tomb more than 2,000 years old. The picture lived in the loom's cords, as yours lives on a card.

note.title: Jacquard's Loom
note.text: Joseph-Marie Jacquard, a Lyon weaver's son, built his loom out of what others had found. In Paris he studied a loom by Jacques de Vaucanson, the maker of a famous mechanical duck, and joined its ideas to Falcon's chain of cards. His loom of 1804 let one weaver weave the richest pattern with no helper at the cords. By 1812 some 11,000 of them were working in France.

note.title: The Woven Portrait
note.text: In 1839 a Lyon workshop wove a portrait of Jacquard on one of his own looms, from some 24,000 cards. It was silk in black, white and every grey between, and so fine that two members of London's Royal Academy took it for an engraving. Charles Babbage, who was designing a calculating machine that would read cards, hung a copy in his home and showed it to his visitors.
